title: Long is the night (60–63)
hook: long is the night to the sleepless; the fool who knows he is a fool is wise so far

segments.voice: Yesterday, paduma, the lotus on the rubbish heap, and your line: the lotus on the heap. What beauty did you find in a rough place? Day one hundred seventy-one, and chapter five: the fool.

Three in the morning, wide awake, and the clock seems broken. Every time you check, it's been four minutes. Or the last mile of a long hike, when your feet hurt and the trail keeps going, and that mile feels longer than the first five. Time stretches when things hurt. The fifth chapter of the Dhammapada begins with exactly those two pictures, and then adds a third that's much less comfortable. Today, verses sixty to sixty-three: long is the night.
screen: `3AM, AND THE CLOCK IS BROKEN.` → `THE LAST MILE OF THE HIKE.` → `A THIRD, LESS COMFORTABLE.`

segments.voice: Verse sixty, in Müller's English: “Long is the night to him who is awake; long is a mile to him who is tired; long is life to the foolish who do not know the true law.” Two ordinary pictures, and then the turn. Life itself drags on, round after round, for someone who never sees how things really are. Chapter five is called the fool, bala in Pali. The word also means a child, someone not grown up yet. It isn't about low intelligence. It's about not seeing. Verse sixty-one says it's better to travel alone than with a fool. Verse sixty-two describes one: my sons, my wealth, he thinks, and it torments him, though he doesn't even own himself, let alone his sons or his money. Then comes verse sixty-three, and it's a gift: “The fool who knows his foolishness, is wise at least so far. But a fool who thinks himself wise, he is called a fool indeed.” The commentary tells it with two pickpockets who went to hear the Buddha teach, planning to work the crowd. One of them started listening, and forgot to steal. The teaching went in, and the story says he saw the truth right there. The other stole a coin and went home. His wife, that evening, mocked the first thief for coming home with nothing, calling him wise. And the Buddha, hearing of it, spoke the verse. The one who knew he didn't know was the one who could learn. There's real relief in that. You don't have to be wise to begin. You only have to notice where you aren't.
screen: `THE NIGHT, THE MILE, THE LIFE.` · `BALA — THE ONE WHO DOESN'T SEE.` · `MY SONS, MY WEALTH.` · `TWO PICKPOCKETS AT A SERMON.` · then, large: `WISE SO FAR.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Now, with no shame at all, bring to mind one thing you don't really know, but sometimes act as if you do. A topic you nod along to. A skill you bluff. Something about the people you love that you've assumed and never asked. Just see it. Let yourself be the first pickpocket, the one who forgot to steal because he started listening. See whether admitting it brings any ease, a small weight put down. Rest there with the breath. The bell holds the time.
Bala. Fool, or child: the one who doesn't see, for whom the night is long, the mile is long, and life itself drags on; knowing it is already wise so far.
Your line: wise so far. Today, say out loud, to someone, one thing you don't know. “I don't know” counts. Day one hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Buddhist teachers often quote verse sixty-three to encourage humility in study, and the story of the two pickpockets is a popular teaching tale.

match.prompt: match the pieces of verses sixty to sixty-three.

myth: in the Dhammapada, 'fool' means someone of low intelligence
bala is someone who doesn't see how things are; the word also means a child.
verse sixty-three says the fool who knows his foolishness is wise so far
the one who thinks himself wise is the real fool.
verse sixty-two says the fool doesn't even own himself, let alone sons or wealth

fork.setup: you're a pickpocket in a crowd listening to the Buddha. the teaching starts to reach you. what does the story say happened?
options: you steal anyway; that's what you came for.
you listen, forget to steal, and see the truth.
you leave before it gets to you.
fork.reveal: one thief listened and was changed; the other stole a coin. at home, the second thief's wife mocked the first as 'wise,' and the Buddha spoke verse sixty-three.

original.note: Pali: fool, and also child: the title of chapter five.

trapdoor: what you thought: 'the fool' in the Dhammapada means stupid people.
what it means: someone who doesn't see how things are; knowing that you don't see is the start of wisdom.
what a scholar hears: verse 63 turns on 'balo mannati balyam, pandito vapi tena so': the fool who recognizes his folly is to that extent a pandita, the word for the wise in chapter six.
